## Approach Deliverable

### Overview

For this assignment, I will use the [Open-Meteo Historical Weather API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) to retrieve daily temperatures and total precipitation for New York City. I will examine data from October 1 to 26, 2026, with the same dates in 2025 to compare if this fall has been warmer than last year. I anticipate some data cleaning challenges, including parsing the JSON, extracting nested daily data, and ensuring dates and measurements are formatted consistently. I will use R to transform the results into a tidy data frame and calculate average daily high temperatures for each period.

## Code Base Deliverable

### Load libraries

```{r}
library(httr2) #httr2 makes the API request
library(jsonlite) #jsonlite parses the JSON response
library(tidyverse) #tidyverse for data cleaning and transformation
```

### Data and transformations

Build the request

```{r}
# Define the API endpoint
url <- "https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive" #url identifies the API endpoint

# Build the API request
request <- request(url) |> #request(url) starts building the request
  req_url_query( #req_url_query() adds the parameters that tell the API what data to retrieve
    latitude = 40.7128,
    longitude = -74.0060,
    start_date = "2025-10-01",
    end_date = "2026-10-26",
    daily = "temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum", #daily requests the daily maximum temperature and total precipitation
    temperature_unit = "fahrenheit",
    timezone = "America/New_York"
  )
```

Send the request

```{r}
# Send the request and retrieve the response
response <- req_perform(request)

# Check the HTTP status code
resp_status(response)
```

Parse the JSON

```{r}
# Parse the JSON response
weather_data <- resp_body_json(response)

# Inspect the structure
str(weather_data, max.level = 2)
```

Convert into dataframe

```{r}
# Extract data into a data frame
weather_df <- tibble( # Opting for tibble() for cleaner data previews and compatibility with tidyverse
  date = unlist(weather_data$daily$time), #unlist() converts each list into a simpler vector
  max_temp = unlist(weather_data$daily$temperature_2m_max),
  precipitation = unlist(weather_data$daily$precipitation_sum)
)

# Preview the data
head(weather_df)
```

Check df

```{r}
# Check column types
glimpse(weather_df)

# Count missing values in each column
weather_df |>
  summarise(
    across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))
  )
```

Convert date column

```{r}
# Convert date column to Date format
weather_df <- weather_df |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))

# Check updated column types
glimpse(weather_df)
```

Filter October data

```{r}
# Filter to October 1–26 in 2025 and 2026
october_df <- weather_df |>
  filter(
    format(date, "%m-%d") <= "10-26",
    format(date, "%m") == "10",
    format(date, "%Y") %in% c("2025", "2026")
  )

# Check the filtered data
october_df
```

Calculate October averages

```{r}
# Calculate average daily high temperature by year
october_summary <- october_df |>
  mutate(year = format(date, "%Y")) |> #mutate() creates a year column from each date
  group_by(year) |> #group_by(year) separates the observations into 2025 and 2026
  summarise( #summarise() calculates the average daily max temp for each year
    avg_max_temp = round(mean(max_temp), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

october_summary
```

Plot line graph

```{r}
# Plot daily maximum temperatures by year
october_df |>
  mutate(year = format(date, "%Y")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = as.integer(format(date, "%d")),
             y = max_temp,
             color = year)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily High Temperatures in NYC",
    subtitle = "October 1–26, 2025 vs. 2026",
    x = "Day of October",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°F)",
    color = "Year"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Conclusion

The Open-Meteo Historical Weather API provided daily maximum temperatures and total precipitation for New York City. I extracted the nested JSON data into a tibble, and checked column types and missing values. I converted the date column to Date format, and because no missing values were found, no additional cleaning steps were taken.

The analysis found that the average daily maximum temperature from October 1–26 was 67.87°F in2026, compared with 66.53°F in 2025, a difference of approximately **1.34°F.** The line graph showed daily temperature fluctuations in both years, but temperatures in 2026 generally remained higher after around October 10, while temperatures in 2025 declined and did not return to their earlier highs.

Future improvements could include automating the date range so the code retrieves data through the current month and day, reducing the need for manual updates. The analysis could also be expanded to include additional years to provide more context on whether these temperature differences are unusual.
